title: This Arctic Town Is Moving Away From Its Own Mine
question: Why do people live in Kiruna?
message: This video tells curious adults that a whole Arctic town is moving a few kilometres east because the iron mine that created it is now eating the ground beneath it, and people would rather move the town than leave it.
angle: People live in Kiruna because iron ore in the hills, known to the Sámi for centuries, and a railway to an ice-free port built a mining town that still supplies most of Europe's iron, and they stay by moving the town itself, despite the mine swallowing the old centre, weeks without sunrise and a move that has cost many people the streets they loved.

scenes.role: lời hứa: thị trấn tên Kiruna, mỏ sắt, lựa chọn dời chứ không bỏ; mở vòng
scenes.narration: The town is Kiruna, in the far north of Sweden, above the Arctic Circle. The whole municipality has roughly twenty-three thousand people, spread over an area about the size of a small country. Under it is a huge iron mine. The mine is slowly swallowing the ground the old town stands on. Most towns would have a crisis. Kiruna packed. Houses, shops, the town hall clock, even a wooden church. By the end of this trip I understood why people would rather move a town than leave it. I also understood that I am terrible at packing. That part I already suspected.

scenes.narration: I arrived in winter with an old paper map and a plan to walk down the main street. The map was a gift from a friend who had visited years ago. He had circled a café and written, best cinnamon buns in the north. I found the main street. It was behind a fence. The shop on my map was gone. The café on my map was a gap with snow in it. I tried another street. Another fence. I began to feel like a man trying to visit a party the day after. Then a sign pointed east, to the new city centre, about three kilometres away. The town had not vanished. It had just moved without telling my map. I folded the map very carefully, the way you fold a letter from someone who has moved away, and started walking.

scenes.narration: Here is what is happening under the snow. The mine digs iron ore deeper and deeper beneath the hill next to town. As it does, the ground above weakens and cracks spread outward. Picture pulling a tablecloth out from under the dinner plates, very slowly, over decades. Sooner or later the plates notice. So the town is stepping off the tablecloth. According to the mining company LKAB, about six thousand people and around three thousand homes have to move. The new city centre was officially opened in September twenty twenty-two. I walked there through the snow. It took me most of an hour, mainly because I kept stopping to look back. Behind me, the old town looked like a stage after the play, with half the scenery already carried off.

scenes.narration: So why build a town this far north at all? My guess was the northern lights. People see a sky like that, they stay. I stood outside that night and waited for proof. I waited with a flask of tea. Then I waited with an empty flask. Then I waited mostly out of pride. The sky did something green and beautiful, and my nose did something numb. Wrong answer, though. The real reason is under my boots. Iron. The Sámi people of this region knew about the iron in these hills for centuries. The town itself was founded in nineteen hundred, as a mining community.

scenes.role: đường sắt tới Narvik 1902 (cảng không đóng băng); Lundbohm, thị trấn kiểu mẫu
scenes.narration: Iron is no use stuck in a hill in the Arctic. You need to get it to the sea. The railway reached Kiruna around nineteen hundred and, two years later, reached Narvik on the Norwegian coast, a port that stays free of ice. That is the whole trick. A hill full of iron, a railway, and a sea that does not freeze. Think of a bakery with a delivery van. Without the van it is just a very hot room full of bread. The mining company's first manager, Hjalmar Lundbohm, is remembered as the founder of the town, and he wanted it to be a model community. I liked him already, and I had not even seen the town he planned. I also liked the bread idea, and was now hungry.

scenes.narration: I took the tour into the mine. It starts small. A single dark pellet of iron ore in my hand, heavier than it looks. Zoom out: a train of wagons full of them. Zoom out again: a mountain with its insides carefully removed. According to LKAB, this is the world's largest underground iron ore mine. The miners are now working about one thousand three hundred and sixty-five metres down. That's well over four thousand feet. The company produces about eighty percent of the iron ore mined in Europe. In twenty twenty-three, LKAB also announced Europe's largest known deposit of rare earth elements right next to the mine. Those are the metals used in magnets for motors and wind turbines. So the town sits on top of something the whole continent depends on. You do not move that. You move the town.

scenes.narration: I went back in August, because I had heard something I needed to see. The church was moving. Kiruna Church, finished in nineteen twelve, was a gift from the mining company to the parish. Big, wooden, red, and much loved. Morning: the vicar gave a blessing. Then the whole church, weighing six hundred and seventy-two tonnes, rolled forward on remote-controlled trailers with two hundred and twenty-four wheels. Speed: about half a kilometre an hour. I walked beside it. I had to keep stopping so I did not overtake it. Children walked beside it. Dogs walked beside it. At one point I am fairly sure a pensioner with a walking frame lapped it twice and went home for lunch. Noon: I bought an ice cream. The church was still in roughly the same postcode.

scenes.narration: Afternoon of the second day: the church arrived. Five kilometres in two days. Thousands of people had come to watch, and when it stopped, they clapped like it had won a race. The company had spent a year widening the road just for this trip. Before the church, twenty-three other historic buildings had already been moved. People whose homes are affected can have a new home built to match, or, where it is possible, have their old house moved across. The new town hall stands in the new centre, with the old town hall's clock tower beside it. Renters get a new place in the new area, and if it costs more, the company pays the difference for eight years. The new centre was planned to be denser, with good lighting, because in a town that spends weeks in darkness, light is a safety feature. Evening: I stood under that clock. It was keeping the same time it always had, just somewhere else. I changed my mind about this place. Moving a town sounded like defeat. Up close, it looked like stubbornness.

scenes.narration: It would be easy to make this a happy story about a church on wheels. It is not only that. Many people in Kiruna are unhappy about the move. Most old buildings are being demolished rather than moved, and for some people, the town they grew up in is simply disappearing. The relocation has also put more pressure on Sámi reindeer herders. They lived in this area long before the mining company arrived, and their herds need open land to move through. And in September twenty twenty-five, LKAB announced that the mine's expansion would require about six thousand more people and around two thousand seven hundred more homes to move. I put the key down on my desk and left it there for a while.

scenes.chapter: Light All Night, Dark All Day
scenes.role: chương 6: mặt trời nửa đêm mùa hè vs đêm vùng cực mùa đông; nhiệt độ; Wob đổi ý lần 2
scenes.narration: Then there is the light. I stayed into the summer, and the sun simply would not set. From roughly the end of May until the middle of July, it stays up all night. At midnight I went for a walk in sunshine, and a bird looked at me like I was the strange one. Then I came back in December. From the start of December until early January, the sun does not rise above the horizon at all. Average temperatures run around minus fourteen Celsius in January, that's about seven Fahrenheit, and around plus twelve Celsius in July. In December, at noon, I made toast in the dark and ate it by the light of my phone. I changed my mind again. Summer, yes. December, I would need a very good lamp and a very good coat. Also a friend who calls every day to tell me the sun is definitely still out there somewhere.

scenes.role: về bàn: ghép các mảnh 'vì sao', phán quyết SUMMER ONLY, callback chìa khoá, câu hỏi kéo bình luận
scenes.narration: So here is how the key fits. Iron in a hill made a town in the Arctic. A railway to an ice-free port made it worth staying. And when the mine started eating the ground, people chose to move the town rather than give up on it, even though it cost them streets they loved. Would I move there? In summer, with the sun up all night and a church strolling down the road, yes. In December, I would want a lamp the size of the church. My verdict is SUMMER ONLY. Unlike the church, I am only moving for part of the year. It suits people who like snow, quiet and a good long project. It does not suit anyone who needs their map to stay true. I hung the key on a hook by my door, next to my own keys, which open things that have stayed exactly where I left them. The door, as far as I know, has not moved. Would you move your whole town to keep your job?

verdict.label: SUMMER ONLY
verdict.reason: Summer brings the midnight sun and a town rebuilding itself with real stubbornness; winter brings weeks without sunrise, deep cold and a town still mid-move.

claims.statement: According to LKAB, about 6,000 people and 3,000 homes in Kiruna need to be relocated.

claims.quote: The new city centre was officially opened in September twenty twenty-two.
claims.statement: Kiruna's new town centre was officially inaugurated in September 2022.

claims.quote: The Sámi people of this region knew about the iron in these hills for centuries. The town itself was founded in nineteen hundred, as a mining community.
claims.statement: The local Sámi knew about the iron ore at Kiirunavaara and Luossavaara for centuries before Kiruna was founded as a mining community in 1900.

claims.quote: The railway reached Kiruna around nineteen hundred and, two years later, reached Narvik on the Norwegian coast, a port that stays free of ice.
claims.statement: The iron ore railway reached Kiruna around 1900 and Narvik, Norway, an ice-free port, two years later in 1902.

claims.quote: The mining company's first manager, Hjalmar Lundbohm, is remembered as the founder of the town, and he wanted it to be a model community.
claims.statement: LKAB's first managing director, Hjalmar Lundbohm, is acknowledged as the founder of Kiruna and wanted it to be a model community.

claims.quote: According to LKAB, this is the world's largest underground iron ore mine.
claims.statement: LKAB describes the Kiruna mine as the world's largest underground iron ore mine.

claims.quote: The miners are now working about one thousand three hundred and sixty-five metres down. That's well over four thousand feet.
claims.statement: LKAB extracts iron ore at Kiruna at a depth of about 1,365 metres (about 4,480 feet).

claims.quote: The company produces about eighty percent of the iron ore mined in Europe.
claims.statement: LKAB produces about 80 percent of the iron ore mined in Europe.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-three, LKAB also announced Europe's largest known deposit of rare earth elements right next to the mine
claims.statement: In 2023 LKAB announced the discovery of Europe's largest known deposit of rare earth elements next to the Kiruna mine.

claims.quote: Kiruna Church, finished in nineteen twelve, was a gift from the mining company to the parish. Big, wooden, red, and much loved.
claims.statement: Kiruna Church, a large red wooden church completed in 1912, was a gift from LKAB to the parish.

claims.quote: Morning: the vicar gave a blessing. Then the whole church, weighing six hundred and seventy-two tonnes, rolled forward on remote-controlled trailers with two hundred and twenty-four wheels. Speed: about half a kilometre an hour.
claims.statement: In August 2025 Kiruna Church, weighing 672 tonnes, was moved after a blessing by its vicar on remote-controlled trailers with 224 wheels at about half a kilometre per hour.

claims.quote: Five kilometres in two days. Thousands of people had come to watch, and when it stopped, they clapped like it had won a race. The company had spent a year widening the road just for this trip.
claims.statement: Kiruna Church was moved five kilometres over two days in August 2025, watched by thousands of visitors.

claims.quote: Before the church, twenty-three other historic buildings had already been moved.
claims.statement: According to LKAB, 23 historic buildings were moved in Kiruna before the church.

claims.quote: People whose homes are affected can have a new home built to match, or, where it is possible, have their old house moved across.
claims.statement: Kiruna residents affected by the relocation can accept a new home built to match their original one or, where technically feasible, have their house physically moved.

claims.quote: The new town hall stands in the new centre, with the old town hall's clock tower beside it.
claims.statement: Kiruna's new city hall in the new centre has the old town hall's clock tower standing next to it.

claims.quote: Renters get a new place in the new area, and if it costs more, the company pays the difference for eight years. The new centre was planned to be denser, with good lighting
claims.statement: In Kiruna's relocation, LKAB finds renters a new home in the new area and pays any rent difference for eight years; the new centre was planned to be denser with good lighting for safety.

claims.quote: Many people in Kiruna are unhappy about the move. Most old buildings are being demolished rather than moved
claims.statement: Many Kiruna residents are unhappy about the relocation, and most old buildings are being demolished and rebuilt rather than moved intact.

claims.quote: The relocation has also put more pressure on Sámi reindeer herders. They lived in this area long before the mining company arrived
claims.statement: Kiruna's relocation has increased pressure on Sámi reindeer herders, who lived in the area long before LKAB arrived.

claims.quote: And in September twenty twenty-five, LKAB announced that the mine's expansion would require about six thousand more people and around two thousand seven hundred more homes to move.
claims.statement: On 25 September 2025 LKAB announced that further mine expansion would require about 6,000 more people and around 2,700 more houses in Kiruna to be relocated.

claims.quote: From roughly the end of May until the middle of July, it stays up all night.
claims.statement: In Kiruna the sun stays above the horizon around the clock from roughly the last week of May until mid-July.

claims.quote: From the start of December until early January, the sun does not rise above the horizon at all.
claims.statement: In Kiruna the sun does not rise above the horizon from roughly early December until early January.

claims.quote: Average temperatures run around minus fourteen Celsius in January, that's about seven Fahrenheit, and around plus twelve Celsius in July.
claims.statement: Mean temperatures in Kiruna are about −14 °C (about 7 °F) in January and +12 °C in July.

claims.quote: Iron in a hill made a town in the Arctic. A railway to an ice-free port made it worth staying.
claims.statement: Kiruna was founded because of iron ore deposits, and a railway to the ice-free port of Narvik made the mining viable.
